agent_1.question: The proposal doesn't say who serves as the rotating steward, how stewards are chosen, or how long each steward's term lasts.
agent_1.answer: I propose that we pick a steward each week by a simple community vote – everyone gets a chance to serve. The person who is steward for that week will review the logbook and enforce the 5 kg trip limit and the 70 % seasonal cap. If a fisher is steward for a given week, they still record their catch but cannot be the one to enforce the rule that week. When a steward’s term ends, the next week’s steward is chosen by the same vote. This keeps the role rotating, prevents power concentration, and keeps all fishers accountable.

Each fisher records their catch in a shared logbook at the dock. A rotating steward reviews the log weekly; if a fisher exceeds the 5 kg limit, they must donate 1 kg of their catch to a communal reserve. If total catch in a season reaches 70 % of the lake’s initial biomass, fishing stops for the remainder of the season. Non‑compliance after two warnings results in a one‑week fishing ban. Steward selection: each week the community votes to elect a steward, and that steward serves for one week. When the steward’s term ends, a new steward is elected for the next week.
agent_1.revised_operationalization: Steward selection and term: At the start of each week, the fishers gather at the dock for a brief meeting. All fishers may nominate themselves or others. The group then conducts a secret ballot or draws names from a hat to choose the steward for that week. The chosen steward’s term lasts exactly one week, ending at the same time the next week’s steward is elected. If the selected steward cannot serve for any reason, the deputy elected in the same vote will step in for that week. All fishers record their catches in the shared logbook; the steward reviews the log each week and enforces the 5 kg trip limit and 70 % seasonal cap. The steward is required to remain impartial and may not enforce rules against themselves in that week.

That person will step in for that week, keeping our rules enforced and the schedule smooth.

agent_2.answer:
The council should set a clear, predictable amount of maintenance work for each repeat violation so that all fishers know exactly what’s expected. I propose that each repeat violation obliges the fisher to perform **4 hours** of boat‑maintenance duties. Those hours can be used for tasks such as cleaning nets, inspecting hulls, tightening fittings, and any other upkeep that keeps the lake and our gear in good shape. The 4‑hour rule is a baseline; if a violation is particularly severe (for example, the fisher caught double the daily limit), the council may decide to increase the hours, but the default remains 4. This ensures fairness, encourages compliance, and directly contributes to the long‑term health of the lake.

The rule also states that the fisher must record the maintenance hours in the shared ledger and complete the tasks within 7 days of the violation. Community members can offer help, but the fisher remains accountable.

agent_3.question: How is the fishery committee constituted and how are its members selected?
agent_3.answer:
The fishery committee is made up of five members who are elected by the fishing community. Every month the fishermen gather at the dock, and any fisher who has been on the lake for at least six months can nominate themselves or be nominated by another. The nominations are put to a simple majority vote, and the top five names become the committee. One of them is chosen as chair by a second vote; the others serve as secretary and treasurer, and two are general members. Members serve a one‑year term and can be re‑elected. If a member steps down or is unable to serve, a replacement is elected by the remaining committee members to fill the vacancy. This way the committee stays close to the people who actually fish and can respond quickly to any issues. Rina’s role is to report her haul and any infractions to the committee in the ledger and to listen to any rules the committee passes. The committee also sits in the chest by the dock to keep the communal pot safe.

The structure is simple: chair, secretary, treasurer, and two general members. All are chosen by vote of the fishing community, and each term lasts one year, with a possibility of re‑election. If a fisher needs to be removed for repeated violations, the committee can vote to suspend that fisher for a day, as specified in the rule.

This system keeps the fishery rule grounded in community participation and accountability.

agent_4.question: What is the procedure for deciding whether a violating fisher forfeits a proportional portion of their catch or must take a rest day, and how is the proportional portion determined?
agent_4.answer: We decide the penalty by looking at how much a fisher went over the rule and how often they do it. 1) If a fisher’s catch is over 8 kg or if the total of all catches would exceed the 15 % lake‑stock cap, we compare the overage to the fisher’s reported catch. 2) The proportional portion forfeited is the ratio of the overage to the total catch that day. 3) If that ratio is small (less than 25 % of the allowed 8 kg or less than 2 kg overage) we simply subtract that fraction of the catch as a fine the next day. 4) If the overage is large—more than 2 kg or more than 25 % of 8 kg—or if the fisher has repeated a violation in the last three days, we require a rest day instead of a fine. 5) The rest day counts as a day when the fisher cannot fish at all, giving the lake time to recover. This keeps the penalty fair, encourages compliance, and protects the lake’s long‑term health.
agent_4.revised_policy: No fisher may take more than 8 kg per trip. The community’s combined daily catch may not exceed 15 % of the lake’s current stock. Before each fishing day we gather, list each fisher’s intended catch, sum them, and if the total would exceed the 15 % limit we proportionally reduce each person’s quota. After each trip each fisher reports actual catch to a community ledger; if someone exceeds 8 kg or the daily cap, the next day they either forfeit a proportional portion of their catch (calculated as the ratio of overage to their reported catch) or, if the overage is large (>2 kg or more than 25 % of 8 kg) or if the fisher has repeated violations, they must take a rest day. The ledger is verified by two independent fishers and kept in a communal ledger box.

Update lake stock estimate daily to recalculate 15 % limit.

agent_4.question: Who is responsible for holding the ledger in the communal ledger box and how is that responsibility assigned?
agent_4.answer:
In our community the ledger keeper is the fisher who writes down the daily catch report and then places the ledger into the communal ledger box.  The duty is not fixed to one person; it is rotated among all fishers on a regular schedule (for example, one fisher per day or one per week), or if the community prefers, it can be decided by a simple majority vote at the start of each fishing season.  The two independent fishers who verify the ledger entries are also part of the rotation, so they know exactly who holds the ledger each day and can confirm its placement.  This way no single fisher has unchecked control over the records and accountability is shared.

We keep the responsibility on the daily keeper and ensure that the ledger is always stored in the communal ledger box after it is verified, so everyone can check it anytime.

agent_4.question: Who is responsible for updating the lake stock estimate each day, and what method or data do they use to compute it?
agent_4.answer: The ledger keeper, together with the community fishers, updates the lake stock estimate each day. They gather the reported catch from all fishers, subtract that total from the previous day’s stock estimate, and adjust for any known natural replenishment or seasonal growth. In practice we use a simple depletion model: we keep a running stock tally, subtract daily catch, then add a fixed or proportionate regeneration amount based on recent trends or a small community survey. If more precision is needed we can bring in a community biologist or use periodic sampling to calibrate the estimate. This keeps the 15 % limit meaningful and reflects the actual state of the lake.

agent_7.question: The proposal doesn't specify who is responsible for enforcing the bans on fishers who exceed the 12kg limit, and how those bans are recorded and tracked.
agent_7.answer: I reckon the Lake Steward should take the lead on keeping the fishers in check.  When someone takes more than 12kg, the Steward records the violation on the shared ledger under a new heading called “Ban Log.”  The Steward then locks that fisher out for the next day, and if it’s a repeat offence the ban stretches to a full week.  The Steward will confirm the ban every morning before a fisher heads out, and the community will get a quick update on the ban list at the daily meeting.  That way the rules are enforced fairly and everyone can see who’s been held accountable.

agent_8.question: The proposal doesn't specify who is responsible for collecting and holding the surplus fish that is added to the community reserve.
agent_8.answer: In practice, the fisher who catches the surplus is the one who brings it back to the dock and deposits it into the community chest.  That chest is kept at the main dock, and a rotating community fish‑keeper—chosen each month from the group—keeps it secure, keeps a physical count, and updates the shared ledger.  So the fisher brings it in, the fish‑keeper stores and records it.
agent_8.revised_policy: Each fisher may take a maximum of 10 kg per trip; any amount above that must be turned over to a community reserve.  The surplus fish is deposited by the fisher into the communal fish chest located at the main dock.  A rotating community fish‑keeper, selected monthly, keeps the chest secure, verifies the amount, and records the transfer in the shared ledger.  The fisher may only keep 10 kg.  If a fisher refuses to comply, the community may withhold trade goods or access to the lake until the rule is respected.  The reserve can be used for community emergencies or to refill stocks before a new fishing season.

The fish‑keeper updates the reserve balance and notifies the community if the reserve reaches a critical level.  Failure to deposit surplus or to log the catch will result in trade restrictions or denied access until compliance is restored.

agent_8.question: The proposal doesn't specify who decides what level of the reserve is considered critical and triggers its use for emergencies or stock refills.
agent_8.answer: I reckon the rotating fish‑keeper, together with the community in our monthly gathering, should set the critical reserve level. For example, we could agree that once the reserve drops below 30 % of its capacity—or any fixed amount like 20 kg—it's deemed critical, and then the reserve can be tapped for emergencies or to refill stocks before a new season. That keeps the rule clear for everyone and makes sure we’re not caught short when trouble comes.

agent_8.question: The proposal doesn't specify who decides whether and how the community reserve is used for emergencies or to refill stocks, or how that decision is recorded in the ledger.
agent_8.answer:
I reckon the whole crew should get a say in how the reserve is spent – especially for emergencies or refilling stocks.  That way no one can take the chest’s fish for themselves when the lake’s in trouble.  The fish‑keeper will still be the one who writes the ledger, but the final decision will come from a vote at the monthly meeting.  Once the community has voted, the fish‑keeper will log the decision with the date, the purpose (emergency or stock refill), the amount taken, and the names of the members who approved it.  That entry will be added to the ledger right after the reserve balance is updated, so anyone can see exactly why the reserve fell below the threshold and what happened to the fish.

In short: the reserve can only be used after a community vote at the monthly meeting, and the fish‑keeper records the vote and the withdrawal in the ledger.

agent_9.question: Who holds and manages the community pot that receives the forfeited 10% of each fisher’s catch?
agent_9.answer: The pot of forfeited 10% is held by the community as a whole and managed by a treasurer chosen by consensus at each monthly meeting.  This person keeps the money in a community trust account and reports on it to the group, ensuring the funds are used for gear repairs or aid to those in need.
agent_9.revised_policy: Each fisher must leave at least 20% of their catch in the lake each trip.  After each trip a fisher calculates 20% of the weight hauled in and releases that portion back into the lake; the remaining 80% is kept.  If a fisher fails to release the required 20%, they must forfeit 10% of their catch to the community pot and pay a small fine.  The pot is held by the community and managed by a treasurer elected by consensus.

agent_9.question: What is the exact amount or calculation for the 'small fine' that a fisher must pay when failing to release 20% of their catch?
agent_9.answer: The fine is 5% of the weight of the catch (rounded to the nearest 0.1 kg).

agent_1.question: What is the required contribution amount and method for fishers who choose to contribute to the fish‑stocking fund after the seasonal cap is reached?
agent_1.answer:
If you choose to contribute after the 70 % cap is reached, you must donate the weight of fish you would otherwise take on that trip – in other words, the full 4 kg you would have caught (or your intended catch if it’s less than 4 kg). The donation can be made in two equivalent ways:
1. Physical deposit: bring the fish to the community fish‑stocking bin at the dock and hand it over to the ledger keeper. The fish will be stored, treated, or released to aid the lake’s stock.
2. Monetary equivalent: if you prefer not to bring fish, you may pay a cash amount equal to the weight (e.g., 1 kg of fish equals 1 silver coin). The council will record the payment and use the funds to purchase fish‑stocking materials.
In both cases the ledger will record the donation as a “stocking contribution” and credit you for that amount toward your seasonal quota, so that your future trips can count the contribution toward the cap. The ledger keeper will verify the entry against your trip log within 24 hours, update the cumulative seasonal total, and flag any over‑catch.
This keeps the fishery sustainable while giving fishers a clear, fair way to support the lake when the cap is reached.

6. The fine for each fisher is 5 % of the sum of (a) their own excess over 10 kg, if any, and (b) their share of the total excess.
7. The monitor deducts the fine amount from the fisher’s recorded payoff for that day and records a “Fine Paid” entry.
8. The deducted amount is transferred to the community reserve fund and recorded in the reserve ledger.
9. The fisher is marked ineligible to fish for the next two days; the ledger prevents any trip entries for that fisher during that period.
10. At the monthly review, quotas are adjusted based on observed population growth.
11. The monitor is elected by majority vote each month and the role rotates among all eligible fishers.
12. The monitor reviews the reserve fund balance, presents any proposed disbursements to the community, and records disbursements only after a majority vote approving the use.

agent_4.question: What is the process the council uses to determine and formalize a new 12% limit when it decides to adjust it?

The ledger shows total catches for the week. Using the latest stock figure, the council calculates a provisional 12 % cap that would allow the lake to recover and maintain the same fish density as the previous week. All fishers then discuss the proposed new cap in the council meeting, weighing recent stock trends, weather, and community needs. The council votes; a simple majority of five or more out of ten is required. Once the vote passes, the new cap is written into the minutes, signed by the chair and all members, and posted to the ledger. The new limit takes effect the following day’s 6 am stock reading. The council also notes the rationale—such as stock below two hundred kilograms, we reduced the cap to ten percent to encourage recovery—in the minutes so future decisions are clear.

The candidate with the most votes serves as steward for one year, then the process repeats. This keeps the steward accountable to the community that relies on the lake.

agent_7.question: The proposal mentions a community keeper who receives surplus fish, but it doesn't specify who the keeper is or how they are chosen.
agent_7.answer:
In our little lake, we’ll call the keeper the ‘Fish Steward.’ I say we pick him by a simple draw each month so everyone gets a turn and no one feels cheated. Anyone who is still fishing that month can toss his name in the hat and the draw will pick the steward for the next month. The steward’s job is to collect any surplus when a fisher catches more than the limit, record it in the shared ledger, and put it into the communal reserve. He must be someone who’s honest, keeps good records, and can stay on the lake during the month. That way nobody gets a personal advantage and we keep the rules clear.

So I’ll restate the proposal with that in place:

No fisher may harvest more than 10 kg per trip; any excess is surrendered to the communal reserve. The surplus is handed over to the Fish Steward, who records the transfer and deposits it into the reserve. The steward is chosen by a monthly lottery among active fishers and must maintain impartiality and accurate records. If a fisher repeatedly exceeds the limit, the community can impose a temporary fishing ban or require a larger share of their catch to the reserve.

The operational details remain: after each trip, you log your catch, give any excess to the steward, and the steward updates the communal ledger. The steward’s identity changes each month by lottery. Compliance is monitored by the steward, who reports any violations to the community council.

This keeps the rule simple, fair, and enforceable without extra bureaucracy. It also means that my aggressive fishing is still rewarded as long as I stay within the 10 kg cap and hand over the rest properly. That’s how we’ll keep the lake healthy and the community in sync.

agent_7.answer: The council that will enforce bans and larger reserve contributions will be composed of three members: the current Fish Steward, who remains impartial; the fisher who has caught the greatest total weight in the past month, to represent active fishers; and a non‑fishing community member chosen by a simple lottery from all residents, to provide outside oversight. They meet on the second Sunday of every month, after the monthly lottery has selected the steward. When a fisher is found to have exceeded the 10 kg limit more than twice in the last month, the steward submits a report to the council. A simple majority (2 of 3) is required for a decision; if the vote is tied, the Fish Steward casts the deciding vote. All council decisions are recorded in the communal ledger and are binding until the next meeting, ensuring fairness and transparency in enforcement.

agent_9.answer: The penalty share goes straight into the community pool. After each trip we gather at the monthly meeting to tally everyone’s catch. Anyone who exceeded their quota must hand the equal share of the overage into the council’s ledger. The council holds the fish (or money) until we decide how to use it – usually for community repairs, gear or a small stipend. If a fisher doesn’t deliver the penalty, the council can impose a fine or suspend that fisher’s next trip. That way the rule is clear and everyone knows where the penalty goes and how it’s checked.

Any fish caught beyond the quota must be released back to the lake. If a fisher exceeds the quota, on the next trip they must give the community an equal share of their catch as a penalty. The penalty share is deposited into the community pool managed by the fishing council and recorded in the communal ledger. Failure to deposit the penalty results in a fine or suspension of fishing permission until the penalty is paid. The rule is reviewed quarterly and adjusted if lake biomass changes significantly.

The council can enforce by requiring payment or revoking a fisher’s permit for a cycle. The policy and its operational details are reviewed quarterly.

The options are lake‑repair costs, gear‑upgrade funds, or stipend money for those who need it.  The committee will publish a short note at each meeting saying how much was taken for each purpose, and all receipts will be kept in the ledger for anyone to check.  This keeps the system transparent and ensures the penalty money actually helps keep the lake healthy and our gear good.

agent_1.question: Who is responsible for measuring the lake’s biomass each month, and what method is used to obtain that measurement?
agent_1.answer: We, the community, agree that responsibility for measuring the lake’s biomass each month will rotate among the fishers, ensuring that everyone has a stake in the data and no single person has too much power. The method will be a simple, repeatable net‑haul survey: every month we will deploy a 10‑meter beam trawl with a 50‑mm mesh over a 5‑km stretch of the lake chosen at random, weigh the catch, and use catch per unit effort (CPUE) to extrapolate to the whole lake. The trawls will be conducted by a small crew of three fishers, supervised by the appointed measurer. All fish caught in the survey are released immediately, so the survey is non‑lethal. The biomass estimate will be recorded and shared at the monthly meeting. If any fisher’s haul exceeds 3 kg, the excess must be returned, and that fisher is barred from fishing the following month. Repeated violations will incur a fee that goes to lake restoration. This keeps the process transparent, equitable, and science‑based while remaining simple enough for us.

agent_1.question: How will the community calculate and enforce the 50% seasonal catch cap based on the latest biomass figure?
agent_1.answer: To calculate the 50 % seasonal cap, we take the most recent biomass estimate (in kg) reported by the rotating trio and multiply it by 0.5. That product is the maximum cumulative amount of fish the community may take during the current season. After each haul we record the weight taken, sum it to a season‑long ledger, and compare the running total to the cap. Once the total reaches the cap, the season’s fishing is suspended for the remainder of that season – no one may fish until the next season or until the cap is reset at the next monthly measurement. Enforcement is carried out by the recording officer who announces when the cap has been met; any fisher who attempts to haul beyond the cap must return the excess, is banned from fishing next month, and repeated violations incur a communal fee that funds restoration.

agent_3.question: How is a fisher’s contribution ratio to the communal reserve calculated for distribution purposes?

The limit applies to the total of all declared catches for that day, and the 10 % figure is refreshed at dawn for the new day.

agent_6.question: Who holds the reserve and how is the reserve balance updated after each fisher’s trip?
agent_6.answer: I keep the reserve as a communal pool that the community accountant manages. After every trip the fisher writes down the total catch; if it’s more than 15 kg, the extra is handed to the accountant. The accountant then adds that excess to the reserve and records the new balance. The reserve must never drop below 200 kg; if it does the whole community stops fishing until the reserve is topped up by the surplus of the next round. If a fisher doesn’t hand over the excess or fishes more than 15 kg, he loses his right to fish the next round until the reserve is back to 200 kg.

agent_1.question: How is a fisher prevented from taking a trip when they are barred, and what happens if they ignore the ban?
agent_1.answer: When a fisher is barred, the facilitator will announce it publicly at the weekly meeting and will keep a ledger that lists banned fishers. We all agree that no one can launch a boat without first checking the ledger. The community normally shares fishing gear and access points; if a banned fisher tries to use the gear, the other fishers will politely refuse. If a fisher ignores the ban and takes a trip, the next time he shows up he will be seen as defiant. The community may decide to revoke his right to fish for the rest of the season, or to impose a larger fine, and will make it clear that continued defiance could lead to removal from the community’s fishing rights. The ban is a social sanction, not a legal one, but we all respect it because our survival depends on it.

agent_3.question: The proposal requires a daily ledger update, but doesn't specify who maintains that ledger or how it is verified—who is responsible for recording each fisher's catch and ensuring compliance?
agent_3.answer: The ledger will be kept by a rotating “ledger keeper” chosen by the community each week. Every fisher records their catch and what they keep on a simple sheet that the keeper collects daily. The keeper updates the shared ledger and circulates it to everyone. To ensure compliance, the community does random spot‑checks and we meet weekly to reconcile totals. If someone forgets to record or exceeds limits by more than 1 kg, the keeper will ask them to donate 1 kg to the reserve.

The reserve is used to seed the lake or support community events.

In the ledger keeper’s role, collecting a 1 kg donation is a simple hand‑to‑hand transaction. After a fisher’s daily record is uploaded, the keeper meets the fisher at the dock (or at the next community gathering) and takes the 1 kg that the keeper records on the ledger. If a fisher refuses, the keeper will first remind him of the community rule and the need for the reserve. Should the refusal persist, the keeper will report the case at the weekly meeting. The community, by majority vote, can then impose a short‑term penalty: the fisher’s personal reserve for that week is reduced by 1 kg and the withheld amount is added to the reserve, or the fisher is temporarily barred from taking a catch until the 1 kg is donated. This is a non‑punitive, restorative measure that keeps the reserve healthy and reminds us all that the lake is a shared resource. The enforcement is thus community‑driven and transparent, not an individual’s power.

agent_4.question: The proposal doesn’t specify how the 3‑day fishing ban is enforced and monitored, or who is responsible for ensuring that a banned fisher refrains from fishing during that period.
agent_4.answer:
The community’s trust is the best deterrent, so the 3‑day ban will be enforced by a rotating "watch" group that comes to the dock each morning. When the Steward issues a ban, the banned fisher must bring a signed card to the dock and show it to the watch. The watch will not allow that fisher to access the boat or net for the duration of the ban, and will record any violation on the shared ledger. If a banned fisher is caught fishing, the ban is automatically extended by another 3 days and the fine is doubled to compensate for the extra damage to the lake’s stock. This way, enforcement is transparent, peer‑regulated, and does not rely on a single person to monitor everyone’s activities.

I propose that the rotating committee be made up of all fishers who own a boat on the lake, with each fisher serving on the committee for one month at a time in a predetermined rotation. The rotation changes every month, and the order is determined by a simple draw at the start of each new year, so everyone knows when their term will be. Committee membership is approved by a simple majority vote of all fishers present at the monthly gathering; if no majority can be reached, the committee defaults to the previous year’s order to keep things moving. This keeps the committee inclusive, transparent, and easy to manage.

The proposed rule is therefore:

"Each fisher may keep up to 20 kg of fish per trip; any fish beyond 20 kg is released into a communal reserve that is used for community fishery maintenance and shared meals, not redistributed. Before each trip, fishers agree on a 20 kg limit. After fishing, the catch is weighed; excess beyond 20 kg is put in the communal reserve. At the end of each month, the reserve is spent on shared tools, fuel, and communal meals; no individual receives a direct share. If a fisher keeps more than 20 kg, the entire catch of that trip is forfeited to the reserve. A rotating committee of fishers monitors compliance and records each trip’s catch."

This policy does not need revision from its previous wording, as the committee details are new.

agent_5.question: How is the 20 kg limit verified and enforced, and what happens if a fisher fails to report or disputes a catch weight?

agent_1.question: What specific restoration work tasks will be assigned to fishers who exceed limits, and how is the required effort determined?
agent_1.answer:
If a fisher exceeds the 2 kg per‑trip limit or the seasonal 25 % quota, the fisher will be assigned restoration work that directly benefits the lake and its surroundings.  The tasks are:
1. Shoreline Clean‑up: 30 minutes of removing debris, litter and small floating trash from a 500‑m buffer zone along the lakeside.
2. Habitat Enhancement: 15 minutes of planting native aquatic and riparian vegetation in designated restoration plots.
3. Gear Repair/Replacement: 15 minutes of fixing or replacing fishing gear (nets, lines, hooks) that has been damaged during the trip.
4. Habitat Structure Installation: 30 minutes of assembling small artificial structures (e.g., log piles, stone walls) that promote fish shelter and biodiversity.
The required effort is scaled to the amount of over‑catch: 1 hour of restoration work for every 1 kg over the 2 kg per‑trip limit, with a minimum of 1 hour and a maximum of 3 hours per trip.  For seasonal over‑catch, the total hours are calculated the same way (1 hour per kg over the 25 % quota).  All restoration tasks are logged in the shared ledger and verified by the Compliance Officer before the fisher may resume normal fishing.

This ensures that exceeding limits carries a tangible, lake‑benefiting cost, encouraging adherence to the sustainable quotas.

agent_2.question: How is a fisher's weekly quota reduced proportionally when they harvest more than 8 kg per trip?
agent_2.answer: When a fisher nets more than 8 kg in a single trip, the amount by which the catch exceeds 8 kg is subtracted from that fisher’s 5 kg weekly personal quota.  For example, if you haul in 10 kg in one go, 8 kg is within the limit and the extra 2 kg is taken out of your 5 kg quota, leaving you with 3 kg to use for the rest of the week.  If you make another trip that also exceeds 8 kg, the new excess is again subtracted from the remaining quota, and so on.  If the cumulative excess reaches or surpasses the 5 kg quota, the fisher’s remaining quota is reduced to zero and that fisher may not fish again until the following week’s quota is reset.  This keeps over‑harvest in check while still allowing fishermen to fish within their allotted allowance.

agent_2.question: What criteria does the committee use to decide whether to adjust the 30% limit up or down during the monthly review?
agent_2.answer: We look at the monthly net survey of the lake’s fish stock and the average daily catch that the community actually hauled in. If the last month’s average daily catch is consistently above about 35 % of the current stock, we lower the limit by 5 % to give the population time to recover. If it is consistently below about 25 % for at least three weeks, we raise the limit by 5 % to allow the community to use the healthy stock more responsibly. If the catch stays between 25 % and 35 % of the stock, we keep the 30 % limit unchanged. We also review regeneration estimates and any ecological indicators that might suggest the lake is more or less resilient before making a decision.

agent_3.question: The proposal doesn't specify who holds the communal reserve and how it is managed or stored.
agent_3.answer: I appreciate your question. The reserve is not just a concept; it is a physical pot of fish that the whole community keeps together. We will store it in the community hall’s cold storage, under a rotating keeper elected monthly by the fisher board. Each fisher will record the catch and the 30% donation in the shared ledger. The board will review the ledger weekly, adjust limits if needed, and enforce compliance. This way the reserve is managed openly and fairly, and everyone knows where their contributions go.
agent_3.revised_policy: Each fisher may keep up to 4kg per trip and 8kg per week; 30% of each trip’s catch goes to a communal reserve; all catches are logged in a shared ledger; weekly reviews determine compliance and adjust reserve share if necessary.

Fish that goes to the reserve is divided into three portions: a short‑term hold for immediate consumption, a mid‑term portion that is dried or smoked for longer preservation, and a long‑term portion that is frozen or salted and stored in a communal pantry. The ledger is a shared spreadsheet (or paper book) maintained by the board clerk; each fisher records catch weight, personal retention, and the amount donated. Weekly board meetings review the ledger, calculate any excess, and enforce the rule. Reserve surplus is earmarked for community food days and for emergencies, and quarterly meetings may adjust the 30% share or personal limits based on lake stock.

agent_3.question: The proposal doesn't specify what enforcement mechanism or penalties exist if a fisher fails to log their catch or fails to donate the required 30% to the communal reserve.
agent_3.answer: In our fishery we trust each of us to be honest, but to make the rule work we need a clear system. We will let the board clerk keep the ledger and do a quick check each week. If a fisher’s log shows a missing entry or a shortfall in the 30 % donation, we first ask them to make the missing donation within the next trip. If they still don’t comply, we require an extra 10 % of the next catch to go to the reserve and we give them a community service day (helping with the cold storage or the community garden). If the same fisher repeats this three times, we suspend their fishing licence for one week, which is a big loss for us all, so it encourages good behaviour. These measures are simple, fair and keep the lake healthy.

All penalties are recorded in the ledger and announced at the monthly board meeting.

If a fisher catches on a Sunday night before midnight, it counts toward that week; a catch on Monday morning counts toward the next week.

agent_4.answer: We’ll let the monitor do a quick stock check each evening. At the end of every fishing day the monitor will take a small sample net (or do a quick visual count) to estimate the total number of fish still in the lake. That estimate is written on the shared ledger and posted in the village square as the lake’s “current stock” for the next day. Every fisher sees that number before they head out, so they know how many fish the lake holds and can plan their catch so the total daily catch stays below 5 % of that stock. The ledger will still record each fisher’s intended catch and actual catch; the monitor checks them and enforces the 3 kg limit and the 5 % rule as before.

agent_5.question: The proposal doesn't specify how the surplus above the 20 kg baseline will be divided and returned to the fishers who met their quota.
agent_5.answer: We’ll split the surplus evenly among every fisher who met his 25‑kg quota that month. That way the extra fish that goes into the maintenance reserve is fairly shared with those who followed the rule.

agent_5.question: When exactly does the monthly audit and distribution of the reserve surplus take place?
agent_5.answer: The audit happens on the first working day after the end of the month, once the reserve has been counted. The surplus is then split and distributed that same day, before any fishers set out for the new month’s trips.

agent_5.question: The proposal says fishers who fail to deposit the excess are penalized with a 5 kg quota reduction next month, but it doesn’t explain how the committee determines which fishers failed to deposit or when exactly the reduction is applied. How will that be decided and enforced?
agent_5.answer:
To know who didn’t put the extra fish in the reserve, the committee will compare two records. Every fisher writes his 25 kg quota on the shared sheet before heading out, and every time he pulls a trip he signs off the amount he keeps and, if any, the weight he takes to the dock. When we dock, the clerk (or the person in charge of the reserve) logs the weight deposited. After the month ends the committee cross‑checks the dock logs with the trip logs. If a fisher’s ‘kept’ weight is greater than 25 kg and the dock log shows nothing or a smaller amount than the excess, that fisher is flagged as non‑compliant. The 5 kg quota cut is applied at the start of the next month’s fishing season, after the committee’s monthly meeting. This way we have a concrete, paper trail for every trip and a clear timeline for enforcement.

agent_6.question: The proposal refers to a community keeper who records catches, calculates lake remaining fish and reserve level, and reviews compliance—who holds that position and how is it appointed?
agent_6.answer: I’m the keeper. The community elected me as the Lake Steward last month during our weekly meeting, by a simple majority of the fishers present. The job’s on a rotating basis so that each fisher gets a turn keeping track of the lake and the reserve. I’m not a fish, but I do sit on the dock with the ledger, check the catch logs, and make sure nobody keeps more than 15 kg per trip and that any extra goes into the reserve to keep it at least 200 kg. If someone fails to follow the rule, I note it, and the fisher loses permission for a week and must add an extra kilogram to the reserve as a penalty.
agent_6.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 15 kg per trip; any excess must be returned to a community reserve kept at a minimum of 200 kg.
agent_6.revised_operationalization: After each trip, the fisher records catch with the keeper. The keeper calculates the lake’s remaining fish and the reserve level. If the lake drops below 200 kg, the fisher must leave fish in the lake to bring it back to 200 kg, and the reserve will be replenished by that excess. The keeper will review compliance weekly; a fisher who fails to return excess will lose fishing permission for one week and must add 1 kg to the reserve as a penalty. Monthly, the community will re‑evaluate the reserve minimum only if the lake consistently stays above 200 kg.

agent_6.question: When a fisher is the keeper for a week, does the keeper also fish that week, and if so, how are they supposed to record their own catch and ensure compliance with the 15 kg rule?
agent_6.answer: Yes, I can still fish when I’m the keeper that week, but I must keep my catch to 15 kg or less. After the trip I’ll write my catch in the keeper log, noting any fish I had to return to the reserve or leave in the lake to keep the lake at 200 kg. The keeper then calculates the lake balance and reserve level to confirm we’re compliant. If I fail to return the excess, I lose permission for a week and must add 1 kg to the reserve as penalty.

agent_6.question: When the lake drops below 200 kg, the proposal says a fisher must leave fish in the lake to bring it back to 200 kg. How is that practically implemented—does it mean releasing caught fish back into the lake, adjusting future catches, or something else, and who monitors/ensures this compliance?
agent_6.answer:
When the lake dips below 200 kg, the rule means I must get the lake back up to that level by putting some of my own catch back into it right after the trip. I’ll release enough fish from my haul so the lake’s remaining stock is 200 kg again, and I’ll note that release in the keeper’s log. I don’t change the rest of the trip – it’s a one‑time release. In the weeks that follow I’ll keep an eye on the lake’s level and take less than the 15 kg cap if it looks like we’re drifting under 200. The keeper keeps the log, does the math, and checks the logs each week. If someone forgets or refuses to release the required fish, the keeper will note the non‑compliance and the fisher loses permission for a week and must add 1 kg to the reserve as a penalty. The community watches the keeper’s weekly report and can spot discrepancies.

agent_6.answer: In this lake we don’t have a big tank – the reserve is kept in a shared holding pen right next to the dock, in a big wooden box with a net and a small bucket of ice for any perishable fish. agent_7.question: Who is designated as the reserve keeper, and what authority does that role have over the communal reserve?
agent_7.answer: The reserve keeper is the community‑appointed steward, a non‑fisher who is entrusted with the communal reserve ledger and the authority to collect the 1 kg of every fisher’s catch, accept any excess fish beyond the 7 kg limit, and enforce the fines outlined in the rule. They may also hold the reserve fish until the community decides how to use it, but they cannot use it for personal profit. They are chosen by the fisher community and are not part of the fishing crew for that round. Their authority is limited to managing the reserve and enforcing the rule; they cannot override a fisher’s trip quota unless a violation is proven.
agent_7.revised_policy: Each fisher may harvest a maximum of 7 kg per trip; 1 kg of every fisher’s catch is automatically allocated to the communal reserve, and any fish taken beyond 7 kg must be surrendered.
agent_7.revised_operationalization: Before each trip, the fisher records intended catch in a shared ledger. Upon landing, the fisher gives 1 kg of the catch to the reserve keeper. A rotating audit crew checks the ledger and catches once a month; any violation results in the fisher forfeiting the next trip’s quota and a fine of 1 kg of reserve fish per extra kilogram over the limit. Compliance is confirmed by a simple signature on the ledger.

agent_7.question: Who composes the rotating audit crew, how are its members selected, and what authority does the crew have to enforce the rule?
agent_7.answer: The crew is made up of fellow fishers who volunteer to serve; each month we rotate a group of three, chosen by a simple draw from all community members who haven’t served in the last three months to keep it fair. Those who serve are trusted members of the community and are given the authority—by the community’s unanimous agreement—to examine the shared ledger, count the fish landed, and enforce the rule. If a fisher violates the limit, the crew can confiscate the excess fish, impose the fine of 1 kg of reserve fish for each extra kilogram, and withhold that fisher’s next trip’s quota until the fine is paid and the fisher signs a compliance statement.

agent_8.question: The proposal doesn't specify how the reserve's stock is tracked—where is the reserve recorded and how are deposits and claims logged in the communal ledger?
agent_8.answer: The reserve is just a column in our communal ledger called the "Reserve". After every trip a fisher writes in their total catch. The ledger then splits that number: the first 2 kg is marked as personal sustenance, the next 8 kg is their personal catch, and anything over 10 kg is entered as a "Deposit to Reserve". If a fisher’s reserve is below 5 kg they can make a "Claim from Reserve" of up to 5 kg, which is also logged. After each entry we adjust the Reserve column by adding deposits and subtracting claims. The chair tallies the Reserve balance after every round and ensures it equals the sum of all deposits minus all claims – that’s how we keep the stock in check.
agent_8.revised_policy: Each fisher must keep a minimum of 2 kg per trip. They may take up to 12 kg of fish, but any amount beyond 10 kg must be deposited into a community reserve. The reserve is used to help any fisher whose reserves fall below 5 kg; such a fisher may claim up to 5 kg from the reserve each trip. If a fisher fails to deposit the required excess, they must surrender 1 kg from their next catch as a penalty. The reserve is tracked in the communal ledger as a separate balance that is updated after each deposit or claim.

After each trip, the fisher records the catch and the ledger updates the reserve balance by adding any excess deposit and subtracting any claim. The chair verifies that the reserve balance always equals total deposits minus total claims. Penalties are logged as a 1 kg deduction from the next trip’s personal catch.

agent_8.question: What constitutes a fisher’s personal reserves, and how are those reserves measured and tracked to determine when a fisher falls below 5 kg and is allowed to claim from the community reserve?
agent_8.answer: Personal reserves are the fish a fisher keeps for future use, not the fish he eats immediately each trip.  We keep a running total of those stored fish in the communal ledger – a column called *Personal Reserve Balance*.  At the start of every trip a fisher’s reserve balance is checked: if it is under 5 kg the fisher is entitled to claim up to 5 kg from the community reserve (the reserve balance will be reduced accordingly).  After a trip the ledger is updated by adding the personal catch (up to 8 kg) to the reserve balance and, if a claim was made, subtracting that claim from the reserve balance.  The 2 kg that a fisher takes for sustenance is removed from the trip’s catch and is not added to the reserve balance.  Thus the reserve balance always equals the total of all personal catches that the fisher has not yet consumed, and it is this number that determines eligibility for a claim.  The reserve itself is a separate ledger column – *Reserve Balance* – which is updated with any excess deposit and any claim, and the chair ensures that it equals total deposits minus total claims.

agent_1.question: What is the weekly catch cap, how is it calculated, and how does it relate to the 50 % seasonal cap for the lake’s biomass?
agent_1.answer:
In practice the weekly catch cap is a dynamic figure that comes from the seasonal cap. At the start of the season we calculate the 50 % of the lake’s current biomass and that is the total amount the community may harvest for the whole 12‑month cycle. Each week we add the catch that all fishers have taken. The weekly cap is simply the amount left of that 50 % divided by the number of weeks remaining. In formula terms:

**Weekly cap = (0.5 × initial lake biomass – cumulative catch to date) ÷ weeks remaining**.

When the cumulative weekly total hits or exceeds the 50 % seasonal cap, everyone stops fishing until the new season begins. This keeps the seasonal limit in check and allows the community to monitor progress. The 3 kg per‑trip limit is still enforced on every individual trip; the weekly cap is a collective safeguard to avoid surpassing the seasonal quota. By recalculating each week we respond to how much has already been taken and keep the lake protected.

agent_1.question: How is the lake biomass estimate obtained, verified, and updated each week, and who is responsible for ensuring its accuracy?
agent_1.answer: We keep the lake’s biomass estimate by gathering data from a small, rotating sample of nets each week. The community leader compiles these figures, checks them against the previous season’s estimates and the observed growth of the lake, and if the numbers look off he asks a trusted elder or a local biologist to double‑check the math. The weekly estimate is then updated by adding the cumulative catch to date, subtracting any natural regeneration we have observed, and dividing by the weeks remaining. Everyone sees the updated number in the community bulletin and we all agree to trust the leader as long as he is transparent about his calculations. If a fisher thinks the estimate is wrong, he can bring it up at the weekly meeting and we’ll revisit the numbers together. The community leader is responsible for ensuring the accuracy, with help from the group of sampling fishers and occasional external verification.

The reset occurs exactly at Monday 00:00, the moment the council is elected and the week’s schedule is renewed. Any catch that a fisher has accumulated during the previous week must be reported by Sunday 23:59; if it is not, it is forfeited to the community pool. At the reset, each fisher’s personal quota of 5 kg is restored, and they may again catch up to that amount during the new week.

agent_3.question: The proposal says a keeper of the ledger rotates weekly, but it doesn't specify who will be the keeper each week or how the keeper is selected.
agent_3.answer: We will choose the keeper by a simple weekly lottery among all fishers. At the end of each week, the community will gather, write each fisher’s name on a slip of paper, mix them, and draw one name. The chosen keeper will be responsible for updating the ledger for the next week. If the drawn name has already served as keeper in the immediate previous week, we draw again to avoid consecutive turns. This keeps the selection fair and transparent and ensures nobody can manipulate the ledger.
agent_3.revised_policy: Each fisher may keep up to 3kg per trip and no more than 6kg per week; 40% of every catch must be donated to a communal reserve; all catches are logged in a shared ledger.

agent_3.question: How is the 40% donation of every catch physically transferred to the communal reserve, and who is responsible for carrying out that transfer?
agent_3.answer:
When I finish a trip I weigh my haul right on the dock. I set aside the 3 kg I’m allowed to keep for myself. From the remaining weight I take 40 % and hand it over to the communal reserve bin that sits beside the storage shed. The keeper of the ledger, who is drawn by lottery each week, checks the two weights, writes them into the shared ledger, and announces the donation amount to the group. If I forget or mis‑measure, the keeper can correct the ledger and issue a notice. The actual transfer—carrying the donated fish to the reserve—belongs to me, the fisher, while the ledger keeper verifies and records the action. This way we keep the process transparent and ensure the reserve grows steadily.

The community has agreed that the person who physically moves the donated portion is the fisher who caught the fish. The ledger keeper’s role is to verify, record, and inform. This procedure works under the current proposal.

agent_4.question: What mechanism does the community use to track and verify the combined daily catch to enforce the 12% lake-stock limit?
agent_4.answer: We keep a communal ledger at the dock where every fisher records the weight of their haul. A rotating community monitor uses a calibrated scale to weigh each catch and cross‑checks the fisher’s report. At the end of the day the monitor sums all logged weights and compares the total to 12% of the lake’s current stock (the stock at the start of the day). If the total exceeds 12%, the excess fish are returned to the lake or the offending fisher is asked to give back part of the haul. The ledger is reviewed at a nightly meeting to resolve any discrepancies, ensuring that the 12% limit is enforced.

agent_5.answer: The 10% penalty will be measured in fish weight, not money. If a fisher fails to hand over the excess beyond 30 kg, we’ll calculate 10% of that unreturned weight and add that amount of fish to the communal reserve ledger as a penalty entry. This keeps the system simple – we’re still dealing with fish, not cash – and the reserve keeper can immediately see the extra weight added to the reserve. The ledger will record the penalty as a negative adjustment to the fisher’s deposit, so the fish count is clear and enforceable.

Each fisher records his catch on a sheet, signs it, and deposits any excess with the reserve keeper before leaving. The reserve keeper may only withdraw fish when a valid request is presented and the ledger is updated.

If anyone spots a mistake or missing entry, they report it to the reserve keeper and we’ll work together to fix it. If we can’t agree within 3 days, the community council will step in to decide. That way we keep the ledger honest and avoid disputes.

agent_6.question: Who is designated as the community monitor and what authority does that person have to enforce the deposit rule and confiscate excess fish?
agent_6.answer: The monitor is the fisher chosen by the community – usually the most senior or trusted member, elected each season. Their job is to keep a log of every haul, check that no one exceeds the 12‑kg cap and to hold the deposit container at the dock. Because the rule is part of the community agreement, the monitor has the authority granted by the consensus to confiscate any excess fish and to suspend a fisher’s right to fish for two trips if they break the rule.
agent_6.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 15 kg per trip; any excess must be returned to a community reserve kept at a minimum of 20 kg.

agent_6.question: What is the intended per-trip harvest limit: 15 kg or 12 kg?
agent_6.answer: The limit is 15 kg per trip – that’s the maximum I let myself keep; anything above that goes back to the reserve.

agent_6.question: What is the procedure for monitoring, recording, and enforcing the reserve level to ensure it never falls below 20 kg, including how reserve levels are tracked and updated when fish are deposited or harvested?
agent_6.answer: Hey folks, to keep the reserve from dipping below 20 kg we’ll set up a simple system.  Each time you finish a trip you’ll first take your 15 kg (or less) and then any extra you haul will be poured into the community pool.  We’ll have one designated spot on the dock— a sturdy bucket or net— that’s our reserve.  Every deposit gets a quick write‑up on the ledger next to the dock.  I’ll be the keeper, but anyone can verify the numbers and sign the page.  After every haul, the keeper updates the ledger: total reserve = previous reserve – any fish taken from reserve + any excess deposited.  We’ll keep a gauge on the pool to eyeball the level and compare it to the ledger.  If the reserve ever drops to 20 kg, no one may take fish from the pool until the reserve is topped up again.  Anyone who tries to slip fish out of the reserve below 20 kg will be fined a portion of their catch for the next trip.  This way we all know exactly how much is in the reserve and can enforce the rule together.

• Enforcement: Any attempt to take fish from the reserve below 20 kg triggers a penalty— a share of that fisher’s catch is forfeited for the next trip.

agent_7.question: The proposal doesn't specify who holds the communal pot (the reserve) or how the 1 kg deposits are managed.
agent_7.answer: The communal pot is kept in a shared reservoir that the community collectively manages. After each trip a fisher deposits 1 kg into that reservoir and records the deposit on the shared ledger. A rotating treasurer—chosen by the community each round—holds the pot in a sealed tank and ensures the ledger balance matches the physical reserve. Any fish taken beyond 8 kg must be returned to that same reservoir before the trip ends. The rotating observer checks the ledger entries, the 1 kg deposit, and the surrender of excess; any breach results in forfeiture of the catch for that round and a one‑round fishing ban.
agent_7.revised_policy: Each fisher may harvest a maximum of 8 kg per trip; 1 kg of every fisher’s catch is automatically allocated to the communal reserve, and any fish taken beyond 8 kg must be surrendered to the reserve.
agent_7.revised_operationalization: Every fisher logs their catch on the shared ledger and immediately deposits 1 kg into the communal pot. Failure to comply results in the fisher forfeiting their catch for that round and being barred from fishing for the next round.

agent_7.question: The proposal doesn't specify how the community selects the rotating treasurer or observer each round.
agent_7.answer: We’ll keep it simple and fair: at the start of each round we’ll gather all fisher names on slips of paper, put them in a hat, and draw one slip for the treasurer (the one who records and collects the 1 kg pot) and another for the observer (who checks the logs). If the same fisher’s name comes up twice, they’ll hold both duties that round – that’s fine as long as they’re honest. The draws are announced to everyone so no one can game the system. This way we avoid bias, keep the process transparent, and no one can hold a permanent position.

agent_8.question: The proposal refers to a community reserve and to fishers’ reserves falling below 5 kg, but no mechanism is specified for creating, tracking, or distributing these reserves—how will individual reserves be defined, tracked, and how will the reserve be allocated to those below the 5 kg threshold?
agent_8.answer: Hey, to keep the system honest, we’ll set up a small ledger. After every trip I jot down how many kilos I have left on my boat – that’s my personal reserve. At the dock, we’ll have a community board where every fisher writes how many kilos they throw into the reserve (anything above 10kg) and how many they pull out. The reserve itself is just a barrel or a bucket where we keep those extra kilos. Whenever a fisher’s personal reserve drops below 5kg, they can ask to take fish from that barrel, up to the amount needed to bring them back up to 5kg. The board shows who’s taken what, so nobody can cheat. That way we all know how much is left in the community reserve and who’s eligible to use it. No more mystery, just a clear paper trail.

3. Tracking: The ledger lists (a) the weight added to the reserve, (b) the weight taken from the reserve, and (c) each fisher’s personal reserve after the trip. This is refreshed daily.
4. Allocation: If a fisher’s personal reserve is below 5 kg, they may request from the community reserve enough fish to bring their reserve back up to 5 kg. Requests are honored on a first‑come, first‑served basis until the reserve is depleted or the fisher’s need is met.

That ledger sits on the dock for all to see. If the ledger shows a fisher has taken more than 12 kg or left less than 2 kg on the boat, the group will notice it immediately. We’ll then call that fisher over and ask them to correct the entry. If they can’t or won’t, the excess fish must be returned to the community reserve and the fisher will lose the right to fish on the next trip until their personal reserve is back at 2 kg. To add a layer of trust, we’ll have a rotating “watchman” who checks the weight on each boat as it leaves the dock and confirms it matches the ledger. This way, the community can rely on the numbers and we all stick to the limits without needing a single person to police us all at once.

agent_9.question: Which existing institutional mechanism (e.g., which phase or role) will be used to determine a violation of the minimum leave requirement, decide on the penalty, and enforce it, and what exactly does that penalty entail (type, duration, enforcement method)?
agent_9.answer: The rule will be enforced through our weekly Community Review Meeting, where the Ledger Auditor reviews each trip’s recorded catch. If a fisher is found to have left less than the required 1 kg, the Community Council will impose a 7‑day fishing ban on that fisher, and, as a secondary penalty, require the fisher to release an amount of fish equal to the deficit (e.g., if 0.5 kg short, they must release 0.5 kg). The ban is enforced by the Community Enforcement Officer who will check the fisher’s gear and prohibit entry to the lake during the ban period.
agent_9.revised_policy: Each fisher may keep at most 8% of the lake’s current biomass per trip, capped at 3 kg, and must leave at least 1 kg in the lake. All catch is recorded on the shared ledger; violations trigger a penalty.
agent_9.revised_operationalization:
1. Before each trip, estimate lake biomass from recent community data.
2. Calculate 8% of that biomass; if >3 kg, cap at 3 kg.
3. Keep at least 1 kg of the caught fish; the remainder (up to the 3 kg limit) is taken home.
4. Record the exact amount taken and left on the shared ledger.
5. At the weekly Community Review Meeting, Ledger Auditors verify the ledger.
6. If a fisher’s recorded left amount is <1 kg, the Community Council imposes a 7‑day fishing ban and orders release of the missing kg, enforced by the Community Enforcement Officer.

agent_9.answer: The Ledger Auditor will be selected on a rotating basis from the pool of fishers who have not served as auditor in the past three months. The Community Council will be elected annually by secret ballot of all active fishers, with the top four vote‑receivers forming the council. The Enforcement Officer will be appointed by the Council from among fishers who have served either as Auditor or as a Council member, and will serve until the next Council election. This system keeps the roles impartial, ensures broad participation, and allows for accountability through rotation.

agent_9.answer: Any fisher who keeps more than the allowed 8% of the lake’s current biomass per trip, or more than 3 kg (whichever is lower), is in violation. agent_9.question: Who is responsible for estimating the lake’s current biomass from recent community data before each fisher’s trip, and how is that estimate derived?
agent_9.answer:

agent_3.question: What criteria are used to determine which community members are considered 'in need' for the weekly distribution of the communal reserve?
agent_3.answer: In this lake community we decide who is "in need" by looking at a few simple things that show a fisher or family is struggling. First we look at how many trips they’ve taken in the last month – if someone hasn’t been able to go out at all because they have no boat, or they’re sick, that tells us they’re in a tight spot. Second we check the number of people in their household – a single parent with children or an elder who can’t leave the house is automatically considered in need. Third, we look at their contribution to the reserve – if they’ve donated less than 25 % of their catch over the last week, that’s a sign they’re not getting enough fish to eat. Finally we ask for a short note if they have an extra expense that week (medicine, school fees, repairs). Anyone who meets at least one of these three marks gets a share of the weekly reserve, and we keep the list updated in the shared ledger so everyone knows who is receiving food. This way we try to be fair to those who can’t fish or have extra burdens.

The resulting figure is taken as the lake’s current stock for that day, and 4 % of that figure is the maximum a single fisher may take on a trip that day, while 8 % of that figure is the total that the community may take that day.

agent_8.question: The proposal doesn't specify how a fisher’s reserve is defined, how deficits are calculated, or how that information is used to determine allocation from the community reserve.
agent_8.answer:
Hey there, I get why this is confusing. The "reserve" I mean isn’t a separate storage box – it’s just the fish you keep in your own stash after each trip. So for each fisher:

1. **Personal reserve** = total weight of fish you’ve stored in your personal space after every round.  That’s the number we look at at the end of the round.
2. **Deficit** = 5 kg – personal reserve, but only if the reserve is below 5 kg.  If you already have 5 kg or more, your deficit is 0.
3. **Allocation from the community reserve** = the reserve is split among all fishers with a deficit, in proportion to each fisher’s deficit.  For example, if the reserve has 20 kg, and the total deficit across all fishers is 10 kg, a fisher with a 3 kg deficit gets 6 kg (3/10 of the reserve).
4. **After the allocation** the community reserve is reduced by the amount distributed, and each fisher’s personal reserve is updated accordingly.

That’s how we use the 5 kg threshold to decide who gets a share and how much.

I’ve written the policy again below with those clarifications. I didn’t change any of the limits on how much you can take each trip or the 2 kg minimum for yourself – just added the missing definitions.

Let me know if anything still isn’t crystal clear.

- **Deficit**: if a fisher’s personal reserve is less than 5 kg, the deficit is 5 kg minus the reserve; otherwise the deficit is 0.
- At the end of the round, the community reserve is allocated to fishers with a deficit, with each fisher receiving an amount proportional to their deficit relative to the total deficits of all fishers.

agent_9.question: Who records the lake’s biomass before each trip, and how is that record verified and logged in the communal ledger?
agent_9.answer: In our small community, the person who records the lake’s biomass before each trip is the fisher who is going out that day. They stand by the bank, take the latest reading from the shared biomass gauge (or a simple visual estimate if no gauge is available), and write down the figure on the communal ledger card. Each entry must include the date, time, and the fisher’s name, as well as a quick signature from another fisher present. That second fisher acts as the verifier: they check the gauge or the estimate against what the first fisher recorded and sign off that it matches. Once verified, the entry is sealed in the ledger, which is kept in the community hall and is also photocopied into a shared digital folder so that everyone can see the record. The ledger is the official record for the trip, so the catch is logged under the fisher’s name, the lake’s remaining biomass after the catch is calculated, and any excess that would leave the lake below 2 kg is returned immediately and noted in the ledger. This two‑step check ensures no one can over‑claim or leave the lake too depleted.

agent_9.question: Who composes the community council that reviews the ledger weekly, and what powers does it have to enforce compliance?

We pick four or five people – one from each of the main fishing households – and we rotate the chair every month.  They’re not politicians; they’re fishermen who know the lake and the work.  Their job is to read the ledger, spot any discrepancies, and make sure every fisher follows the rule.  If someone breaks the 2‑kg rule, the council can order the fisher to return the excess fish, hand the caught fish to the community pot to be used for repairs or the communal stew, or if it’s a repeat offence, suspend that fisher’s right to fish for a week or two.  The council’s authority comes from the agreement we all made at the last meeting – we all sign a pledge that we’ll respect their decisions.

We do not have a police force or a court; we use simple checks and a small fine that goes into the communal maintenance fund.  The council’s power is to enforce compliance through restitution, fines, and temporary suspension, and to change the rule if the lake’s health or the community’s needs change.

We keep the ledger in the hall, back it up digitally, and everyone signs the entries.  The council meets every Saturday, reads the ledger, speaks with any fishers who had a problem, and records any penalties or corrections.  That’s how we make sure the lake stays healthy and everyone gets a fair share.

agent_0.policy: Daily total catch may not exceed 30% of the lake’s current stock (or 10 kg, whichever is lower), and no fisher may take more than 2 kg per trip.
agent_0.operationalization: Each fisher records their catch in the communal logbook before and after fishing. At the end of each day the community totals the lake catch and checks against the 30% (or 10 kg) cap. If the cap is exceeded, the excess fish are returned to the lake and the exceeding fisher forfeits the overage. Any fisher taking more than 2 kg must surrender 1 kg of their haul. A fisher who repeatedly violates the rule receives a one‑day fishing ban. The rule is reviewed and possibly adjusted every three months based on lake stock changes.
agent_0.reasoning: The 30% cap keeps the lake’s stock in a sustainable range while the 10 kg hard limit protects the lake when the stock is low. A 2 kg per‑trip limit guarantees that every fisher can get at least 1 kg for themselves without risking over‑exploitation. The logbook and simple penalties give the community clear, enforceable oversight, preserving the lake for future generations.

agent_1.policy: The lake may be fished only to a total seasonal catch of 30% of its current biomass, and each fisher may take no more than 2 kg per trip.
agent_1.operationalization: Before each season we calculate the lake’s biomass and set a 30% seasonal quota. Each fisher receives a 2 kg token and records catch on a shared ledger after every trip. If a fisher exceeds 2 kg or the season’s total catch passes 30%, the excess is returned to the lake and a small fine is imposed. Violations are reported to the council and the lake’s reserves are adjusted accordingly. Remaining biomass is reserved for natural regeneration and a restocking fund.
agent_1.reasoning: This keeps the lake healthy for future generations, ensures fairness, and gives each of us enough to survive while protecting the fish population.

agent_2.policy: The lake may be fished no more than 20% of its current stock per day, no individual may take more than 5 kg per trip, and each fisher is limited to 15 kg per week; all catches must be reported within 24 hours to a shared ledger.
agent_2.operationalization: Each morning fishermen log intended catch; if total intended exceeds 20% of measured stock, all trips are scaled down proportionally. Each fisher’s weekly total is tracked; once 15 kg is reached, they must wait until next week. Failure to record or exceed limits incurs a community fine; fines fund a lake restoration reserve.
agent_2.reasoning: The 20% cap keeps biomass above a critical threshold; 5 kg per trip reduces burst pressure; a 15 kg weekly quota limits seasonal over‑catch; reporting and fines enforce compliance and build a restoration fund, ensuring long‑term lake health.

agent_3.policy: Each fisher may keep up to 4 kg per trip and no more than 8 kg per week; 30 % of every trip’s catch must be donated to a communal reserve; all catches are logged in a shared ledger and reviewed weekly.
agent_3.operationalization: After each trip, a fisher records trip weight, personal haul, and reserve share in the ledger. At the end of the week, the ledger is tallied: if any fisher exceeds 8 kg, 50 % of the excess is automatically transferred to the reserve and the fisher is barred from fishing the next week. Any fish not logged or misreported is treated as a violation and the fisher must donate 100 % of that catch to the reserve. The reserve stock is reviewed monthly to adjust the 30 % share up or down by ±5 % to maintain lake health, and the community collectively votes on any change.
agent_3.reasoning: I’m proposing this because it balances personal survival needs with community sustainability. The 4 kg per trip keeps the reserve safe, the weekly cap prevents over‑harvest, and the 30 % reserve share replenishes the lake. Logging and weekly review keeps accountability high, and penalties encourage honesty. Adjusting the reserve share based on lake stock ensures we don’t push the lake below a safe threshold, protecting everyone’s future income.

agent_4.policy: Each fisher must catch at least 1 kg per trip but no more than 5 % of the lake’s current stock per trip, and the community’s combined daily catch may not exceed 10 % of the lake’s current stock.
agent_4.operationalization: At the start of each day the community gathers to announce the lake’s current stock. Every fisher records their catch on a shared ledger. If a fisher’s catch exceeds 5 % of the lake stock, they must return the excess to the community’s shared pool. If the community’s total catch exceeds 10 % of the lake stock, the excess fish must be redistributed equally among all fishers or donated to those unable to catch 1 kg. Non‑compliance results in a penalty of one day’s catch being forfeited to the pool and the fisher’s next trip postponed until the penalty is paid. The ledger is reviewed weekly and any disputes resolved by community vote.
agent_4.reasoning: The lake is only at about 32 kg, so higher per‑trip limits risk depleting the population. A 5 % cap keeps individual catches around 1–1.5 kg, enough for sustenance yet limiting over‑exploitation. The 10 % community cap ensures the lake’s stock is preserved for future seasons. By requiring transparent logging and community enforcement, we protect the lake and maintain fairness among all fishers.

agent_5.policy: Each fisher may keep up to 30 kg of fish per trip; any fish beyond 30 kg is deposited into a communal maintenance reserve for lake upkeep and shared meals.
agent_5.operationalization: On each trip, a fisher records the weight of fish caught and claims up to 30 kg as personal haul. If more than 30 kg is caught, the excess is marked and placed in a communal bin. At the end of each month, the communal reserve is tallied and used solely for lake maintenance projects and community meals; fishers do not redistribute the reserve. Failing to return excess fish results in a 10 % penalty of the fisher’s next catch being added to the reserve.
agent_5.reasoning: I want to keep my catch maximum while still respecting the lake’s shared nature. A 30 kg limit protects the lake and satisfies the community, and the communal reserve ensures maintenance and meals. This rule lets me keep almost all of my haul, and the small penalty deters abuse.

agent_6.policy: Each fisher may keep up to 15 kg per trip, depositing 5 kg into a communal reserve that is maintained at a minimum of 20 kg.
agent_6.operationalization: On each trip, a fisher records the total catch at the community station before leaving. They keep up to 15 kg; if they catch more, they must bring the excess 5 kg to the reserve. The reserve is tracked by the community council and cannot drop below 20 kg. If a fisher fails to deposit the required amount or keeps more than 15 kg, they must forfeit one upcoming trip and the excess fish will be redistributed among the community. All fished fish are counted toward the reserve after each round.
agent_6.reasoning: This keeps enough fish for the community and for me to survive, while giving me a generous catch per trip. The reserve ensures the lake’s health, and the enforcement makes it fair. It also matches the patterns of past proposals, but with a higher reserve threshold to protect the dwindling stock.

agent_7.policy: Each fisher may harvest up to 8 kg per trip, must set aside 1 kg of that catch into the communal reserve, and the lake must never fall below 30 kg; any catch that would drop the lake below 30 kg must be surrendered to the reserve.
agent_7.operationalization: After each trip, the fisher places 1 kg of their catch into the reserve. The remaining catch may only be taken if the lake after removal stays at or above 30 kg; otherwise the fisher must surrender the excess to the reserve. The community council records each trip’s catch and checks compliance. If a fisher fails to surrender the required amount, they forfeit 1 kg of catch, which is added to the reserve, and receive a warning. Peer monitoring and random audits enforce the rule.
agent_7.reasoning: This rule lets me fish enough for survival while protecting the lake from overexploitation. The 8 kg cap limits individual impact, the 1 kg reserve builds a buffer, and the 30 kg floor keeps the lake productive. Enforcement ensures everyone follows the agreement.

agent_8.policy: Each fisher may take up to 6 kg of fish per trip, must keep at least 2 kg for personal sustenance; any fish beyond 6 kg is deposited into a community reserve that is first used to replenish the reserves of any fisher whose reserves fall below 5 kg. The reserve is replenished each week by a mandatory contribution of 1 kg from every fisher who has a personal reserve above 10 kg.
agent_8.operationalization: Before setting out, each fisher declares the amount they will keep (minimum 2 kg). The catch is measured; if it exceeds 6 kg, the excess is taken to the communal bin and logged. At the end of each week, every fisher tallies their reserves; if above 10 kg, they must hand 1 kg to the bin. Reserve funds are released immediately to any fisher whose reserves drop below 5 kg; they receive fish from the bin to bring reserves up to 5 kg. If a fisher fails to deposit the required 1 kg when eligible, they lose priority access to the reserve for that week and must pay a 0.5 kg penalty in the next round.
agent_8.reasoning: I need at least 2 kg per trip to survive and keep my reserves above zero. A 6 kg cap protects the lake from being overfished while allowing me to take enough to earn a living. The community reserve ensures that if my reserves dip, I still have a safety net. Replenishing the reserve with a small contribution from those with surplus keeps it sustainable. The penalty discourages non‑compliance.

agent_9.policy: Each fisher may keep up to 10% of the lake’s current biomass per trip, capped at 3 kg, and must leave at least 2 kg of fish in the lake after each trip.
agent_9.operationalization: At the start of each trip, the fisher notes the lake’s current biomass. The allowed catch is the smaller of 10% of that biomass, 3 kg, and the amount that would leave 2 kg in the lake. The fisher records the catch in a communal log. If a fisher exceeds the allowed amount, the excess is returned to the lake and the fisher forfeits the right to fish for the next two rounds. The community monitors and verifies catches by random checks and peer reporting.
agent_9.reasoning: This keeps the lake stocked, gives everyone a fair chance to catch enough for themselves, and makes sure no one can over‑fish. The 10% cap is flexible as the lake shrinks, the 3 kg cap protects the lake when the biomass is low, and the 2 kg reserve protects the future.
